units.title: What a 3D model is made of
units.blurb: Vertices and triangles, normals and the front face, UVs and materials, the scene, units and axes. You need these to understand any format.

lessons.title: Vertices and triangles
lessons.sub: What every 3D model is glued together from

cards.title: A model is an empty shell
cards.body:
Almost every 3D model in a game or a browser is a thin “skin” with nothing inside. It is glued together from flat pieces.

Think of a paper mask: from the outside it looks like a face, but inside it is hollow.

cards.title: Three words
cards.body:
A vertex is a point in space: three numbers x, y, z.
An edge is a line segment between two vertices.
A face is a flat piece bounded by edges.

A set of vertices and faces is called a mesh.

cards.title: Why triangles
cards.body:
Exactly one plane passes through any three points, so a triangle is always flat. A quad can have one corner “bent out”, and then it is unclear how to shade it.

The GPU draws only triangles, so everything else is cut into them before display.
cards.deep: Modelers love quads: they work better with subdivision smoothing and edge loops. But renderers and glTF get triangles: a quad is 2 triangles, a convex n-gon is n − 2.

cards.title: A mesh has to go into a file
cards.body:
A file format is an agreement on how to write a mesh down: what comes after what and what each number means. There are many formats. You will see their names all the time, so here are the four main ones:

OBJ is an old, simple text format: a list of vertices, then a list of triangles.
STL is the 3D printing format: triangles only, no color or textures.
glTF is the modern format for games and the browser.
FBX is for exchange between tools like Blender, Maya and Unity.

We will cover each one in detail in unit two. For now, one thing matters: different formats write the same mesh in different ways.

cards.title: Two ways to write triangles
cards.body:
OBJ first lists every vertex once, then writes each triangle as numbers: “vertices 1, 2, 3”.

STL has no numbers: every triangle writes out all three points in full. A vertex shared by neighboring triangles is repeated once for every triangle that meets there.

cards.task: Build a house out of triangles: tap three vertices at a time. Below you can see how OBJ and STL would write the same mesh. Count the vertices in each.

cards.q: How many triangles does it take to cover the house, a convex pentagon?
cards.explain: A convex polygon with n vertices splits into n − 2 triangles: 5 − 2 = 3.

cards.q: Why does STL store 9 vertices while OBJ stores only 5?
options: OBJ lists each vertex once and refers to it by number, while STL repeats vertices in every triangle
cards.explain: These are two approaches: an indexed mesh (OBJ, glTF) and “triangle soup” (STL). Indices save space and keep connectivity.

cards.q: Match each word to its meaning
pairs: A point: three numbers x, y, z
A flat piece, usually a triangle
A set of vertices and faces

cards.q: How many triangles does a cube have?
cards.explain: 6 square faces, 2 triangles each.

cards.q: Why does the GPU draw triangles specifically?
options: A triangle is always flat, so it is simple and fast to shade
One manufacturer decided so long ago
cards.explain: A face that is flat with no exceptions is the perfect building block for hardware that draws billions of faces per second.

lessons.title: Normals and the front face
lessons.sub: Why models sometimes have holes

cards.title: A face has a front and a back
cards.body:
The order in which a triangle’s vertices are listed sets its front side. Counterclockwise (as you look at the triangle) means it faces you; clockwise means you see its back.

The GPU usually skips the back side, which saves almost half the work. This is called backface culling.

cards.task: Build the house so every triangle faces you (green). Got a red one? Reverse its winding.

cards.q: In a game, some faces of a model vanished: you can only see them from inside. Most likely…
options: Those triangles have reversed winding, so their normals point inward
cards.explain: Back faces are culled, so flipped faces disappear from the outside. In an editor you fix it by recalculating normals to point outward.

cards.title: A normal is an arrow pointing out
cards.body:
A normal is a unit vector perpendicular to the surface. Lighting uses it: how much the surface is turned toward the light.

In STL each triangle has one normal. In OBJ and glTF normals are stored per vertex, which allows smooth lighting.
cards.deep: There are also normal maps: textures that replace the normal at every point and draw fine detail without extra triangles. To orient such a texture correctly you need tangents.

cards.task: Switch between flat and smooth normals and compare how many vertices the GPU needs.

cards.q: Why does the GPU need more vertices with flat normals?
options: To the GPU a vertex is a position plus a normal; on an edge between faces with different normals, the point has to be stored twice
It is a bug in the demo
cards.explain: The GPU cannot do “one point, two normals”. A sharp edge means duplicated vertices.

cards.q: A cube with sharp edges has 8 corners. How many vertices will the GPU get?
cards.explain: Each corner belongs to three faces with different normals, so it gets three copies: 8 × 3 = 24.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all.
options: The order of a triangle’s vertices sets its front side
glTF treats counterclockwise winding as the front
Normals are needed to compute lighting
A normal is the color of a vertex
The back of a triangle is always drawn
cards.explain: A normal is a direction, not a color. You can turn on back faces (a double-sided material), but by default they are culled.

lessons.title: UVs and materials
lessons.sub: How a picture gets onto a model, and why metal shines

cards.title: How to stick a picture on 3D
cards.body:
To paint a model with a picture (a texture), each vertex gets a second set of coordinates, UV: where on the picture this point sits. U is horizontal, V is vertical, both from 0 to 1.

This is an unwrap: like cutting open a cardboard box and laying it flat on a table.

cards.title: A material is what an object is made of
cards.body:
A material says how a surface reflects light. The modern approach is PBR (physically based rendering): base color, metallic and roughness.

The same numbers look almost the same in different programs, which is why PBR became the standard.
cards.deep: glTF uses the metallic-roughness model: baseColor, metallic, roughness, normal, occlusion, emissive, plus extensions (transmission, clearcoat, sheen). Older formats such as OBJ with .mtl and Collada describe materials with Phong: diffuse, specular, shininess. Those materials transfer poorly between programs.

cards.q: Which glTF line says the material is metal?
cards.explain: metallicFactor = 1 means metal. 0 means a dielectric: plastic, wood, stone.

cards.q: A vertex has UV = (0.5, 0.5). Where is it on the texture?
options: In the center of the picture
cards.explain: Both coordinates are halfway through the 0 to 1 range.

cards.q: metallic = 1, roughness = 0. What does it look like?
cards.explain: Metal with zero roughness reflects like a mirror. The higher the roughness, the blurrier the highlight.

cards.title: Textures inside or alongside
cards.body:
Pictures either sit as separate files next to the model (OBJ + .mtl + .png, glTF + .bin + .png) or live inside a single file (GLB, USDZ, FBX with embedded textures).

Separate files are easy to lose when you send them, hence the eternal “the model arrived gray”.

cards.q: Someone sent you model.obj, and in the viewer it is gray. Why?
options: They did not include the .mtl and textures: OBJ keeps materials separately
cards.explain: OBJ points to material.mtl with an mtllib line, and that file points to the pictures. No files, no color.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Where a point lies on the picture

cards.q: What does a glTF PBR material describe? Select all.
cards.explain: A material is about the surface. Geometry and files are not its concern.

lessons.title: Scene, units and axes
lessons.sub: Why a model arrives 1000 times too big, or lying on its side

cards.title: A file often holds a whole scene
cards.body:
A file stores not one mesh but a tree of objects: car → body → four wheels. Each node has its own transform: translation, rotation and scale relative to its parent.

Rotate the car, and the wheels go with it.

cards.q: Arrange the hierarchy from top to bottom
cards.explain: The wheel is a child of the body, the body is a child of the car, the car is a child of the scene.

cards.title: Units: meters, centimeters or nothing
cards.body:
The number 10 in a file: 10 of what? By spec, glTF is always in meters. FBX stores the scale in the file settings. OBJ and STL store no units at all, so the program has to guess.

Hence the classic “the model arrived 1000 times too big”.

cards.title: Which axis points up
cards.body:
In some programs up is the Y axis (glTF, Maya, Unity); in others it is Z (Blender, 3ds Max, Unreal Engine, most CAD systems).

If you do not rotate the model on export, it will lie on its side.

cards.task: A 10 cm mug is exported without conversion from a Z-up program into a glTF viewer. Pick the settings so the mug stands upright at a normal size.

cards.q: A 25 mm part was exported in inches (0.984). The slicer assumed the STL is in millimeters. What size will it show?
cards.explain: STL stores no units. The slicer read 0.984 as millimeters, and the part became tiny.

cards.q: Why do the wheels move with the car when you move it?
options: The wheels are child nodes: their transform is relative to the parent
The program moves every object in the scene
The wheels are merged with the body into one mesh
cards.explain: The wheel’s final position = the car’s transform × the body’s × the wheel’s own.

cards.q: Which of these use Y up? Select all.
cards.explain: Blender, 3ds Max and Unreal are Z up. Exporters usually rotate the model for you, but not always.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: Final: anatomy of a model
lessons.sub: Vertices, normals, UVs and the scene: test yourself

cards.task: Build the house with every triangle facing you.

cards.q: How many triangles do you get from one quad?
cards.explain: A quad is cut along a diagonal into two triangles.

cards.q: Which OBJ line sets a UV coordinate?
cards.explain: vt is a texture vertex, that is, a UV. vn is a normal, f is a face.

cards.q: A triangle is listed clockwise as you look at it. What do you see with backface culling on?
options: Nothing: its back is facing you
cards.explain: Counterclockwise winding counts as the front.

cards.q: A cube with sharp edges: how many vertices does the GPU need?
cards.explain: Three copies of each corner, one for each face with its own normal.

cards.task: Make the mug in glTF stand upright and be 10 cm tall.

cards.q: What do OBJ and STL not store? Select all.
cards.explain: Every mesh has vertices. But these old formats have no units, hierarchy or animation.

cards.q: A model arrived gray. What do you check first?
options: Whether the material and texture files were included
cards.explain: External textures are the thing most often lost in transit.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: The back side is not drawn

units.title: Meshes: formats for display and exchange
units.blurb: OBJ, STL, PLY, glTF/GLB, FBX, Collada, USD/USDZ: what each can do, where you will meet it, and what gets lost in conversion.

lessons.title: OBJ and STL
lessons.sub: Simple, old and understood by everyone

cards.title: OBJ: a text file from the 80s
cards.body:
Wavefront created OBJ in the late 1980s. It is plain text: a v line is a vertex, vt is a UV, vn is a normal, f is a face made of vertex numbers (counting from one). Materials live in a separate .mtl file.

It opens in Notepad and in almost any 3D program.
cards.code:
mtllib box.mtl
v 0 0 0
v 1 0 0
v 1 1 0
vt 0 0
vn 0 0 1
usemtl Wood
f 1/1/1 2/1/1 3/1/1
cards.deep: f 1/1/1 means the position, UV and normal numbers. A face can be a quad or an n-gon: OBJ does not require triangles. Negative indices count from the end. There is no hierarchy or animation: o and g are just group names.

cards.title: STL: the language of 3D printers
cards.body:
STL was created in 1987 for stereolithography (by 3D Systems). Inside there are only triangles: each has a normal and three vertices. No color, no UVs, no units.

It comes in text and binary flavors. Binary: an 80-byte header, the triangle count, and 50 bytes per triangle.

cards.task: Build the house from front-facing triangles and compare how many bytes and vertices go into OBJ and into STL.

cards.q: Complete the OBJ face from vertices 1, 2, 3
cards.explain: f stands for face. The numbers refer to the v lines in order, starting from one.

cards.q: How big is a binary STL with 1,000 triangles?
cards.explain: 84 bytes of header and counter + 1,000 × 50 bytes: normal 12, three vertices 36, attribute bytes 2.

cards.q: Why is STL still the standard in 3D printing?
options: A printer only needs the shape, and STL is the simplest, most widely understood way to send it
cards.explain: A slicer needs a closed volume made of triangles. STL does not need anything else.
cards.deep: There is also the newer 3MF for printing: units, colors, materials and multiple objects in one zip file. Slicer support for it keeps growing.

cards.q: Which line of the text STL holds the normal?
cards.code:
solid part
  facet normal 0 0 1
    outer loop
      vertex 0 0 0
      vertex 1 0 0
      vertex 0 1 0
    endloop
  endfacet
endsolid part
cards.explain: facet normal is the triangle’s normal, followed by three vertex lines.

cards.q: What gets lost if you save a game character as STL? Select all.
cards.explain: Only the shape, made of triangles, survives.

cards.q: Match the OBJ lines

lessons.title: PLY for scans
lessons.sub: A header that describes itself

cards.title: PLY from Stanford
cards.body:
PLY (Polygon File Format) was created at Stanford in the 1990s, the same place that scanned the famous “Stanford bunny”.

First comes a header: how many vertices, what properties they have (x, y, z, color, normal…), how many faces. Then the data itself, as text or in binary.

cards.q: Which line says how many vertices there will be?
cards.code:
ply
format binary_little_endian 1.0
element vertex 120000
property float x
property float y
property float z
property uchar red
property uchar green
property uchar blue
element face 0
end_header
cards.explain: element vertex 120000 means 120 thousand vertices with the listed properties follow.

cards.q: This file says element face 0. What does that mean?
cards.code:
ply
format binary_little_endian 1.0
element vertex 120000
property float x
property float y
property float z
property uchar red
property uchar green
property uchar blue
element face 0
end_header
options: There are no faces: it is a point cloud
The faces are in another file
cards.explain: PLY happily stores points without faces, which is why scanners love it.

cards.title: Why scanners love PLY
cards.body:
You can give vertices any properties: color, normal, scanner confidence, intensity. There may be no faces at all.

That is why PLY is common in photogrammetry, science and robotics.
cards.deep: 3D Gaussian Splatting models are usually stored in PLY too: each “point” is a Gaussian with its own properties (scale, rotation, opacity, color coefficients). The format allows this with no extensions, just new property lines.

cards.q: A scanner produced millions of colored points. Which of the simple mesh formats fits?
cards.explain: STL stores only triangles without color. PLY stores points with any properties.

cards.q: What can PLY store? Select all.
options: Custom properties, such as scanner confidence
cards.explain: PLY is a flexible table of vertex and face properties. It has no animation or scene.

cards.q: Declare a color property in the PLY header
cards.code:
element vertex 3
property float x
property float y
property float z
property ___ red
cards.explain: uchar is a byte from 0 to 255, the usual type for color.

cards.q: Match the header lines
pairs: The first line of the file

lessons.title: glTF and GLB
lessons.sub: The “JPEG of 3D”: ready to display

cards.title: Ready to display
cards.body:
glTF (GL Transmission Format) is made by the Khronos Group; version 2.0 came out in 2017. People call it the “JPEG of 3D”: a browser, AR viewer or engine can show the model right away, with almost no conversion.

Meters, Y up, PBR materials, hierarchy, skeletal animation: it is all defined in the standard.

cards.title: .gltf or .glb
cards.body:
.gltf is JSON describing the scene, with a .bin file of vertex arrays and texture images next to it.

.glb is the same thing in one binary file. GLB is handier for sending: nothing gets lost.
cards.deep: GLB: a 12-byte header (magic “glTF”, version 2, file length), then a JSON chunk and a BIN chunk. The data sits in buffers, while bufferViews and accessors describe how to read it. The arrays go to the GPU with almost no processing, hence “ready to render”.

cards.q: Which line says where the vertex positions are?
cards.explain: POSITION is the vertex positions. The number is the index of the accessor that says where they are in the binary data.

cards.q: What does the 0 in "POSITION": 0 mean?
options: The index of an accessor, which describes where in the binary data the positions are
The coordinate of the first vertex
cards.explain: The JSON only describes the data. The numbers themselves are in a binary buffer, and the accessor gives the type, count and offset.

cards.title: Extensions: compression
cards.body:
The glTF core can be extended. KHR_draco_mesh_compression and EXT_meshopt_compression shrink geometry several times over. KHR_texture_basisu adds KTX2 textures that the GPU reads without unpacking them into huge RGBA.

This is how 3D on the web gets lightweight.

cards.task: A character with PBR materials and animation has to be shown in a browser. Find the format that keeps everything.

cards.q: Why pick GLB over FBX for the web?
options: It is an open standard, a single file and ready to render; three.js, Babylon.js and AR viewers understand it
cards.explain: FBX is closed and built for exchange between programs, not for fast delivery to a browser.

cards.q: What does the glTF 2.0 spec define? Select all.
options: Layers and variants, as in USD
cards.explain: glTF is about delivering triangles to the screen. Exact CAD geometry and building scenes from layers are jobs for other formats.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: FBX and Collada
lessons.sub: The pipeline workhorse and its open ancestor

cards.title: FBX: the workhorse of game dev
cards.body:
FBX started as the format of Kaydara’s Filmbox and has belonged to Autodesk since 2006. It stores meshes, materials, hierarchy, skeletons, animation, morphs, cameras and lights.

The format is closed. The official way to read it is the free but closed-source FBX SDK. Other programs rely on reverse engineering. Hence “an FBX from Blender looks wrong in Max”.

cards.title: Collada: open XML that never took off
cards.body:
DAE (Collada) was created at Sony Computer Entertainment, then moved to Khronos, the same group that makes glTF.

It is XML: human-readable, but heavy and too flexible, so every program understood it its own way. Today glTF has almost replaced it.

cards.q: Why does an FBX from one program sometimes open with errors in another?
options: The format is closed, and not everyone uses the official SDK, so each program reads it a little differently
Programs break other vendors’ files on purpose
cards.explain: No open spec means no guarantee that everyone reads the file the same way.

cards.q: An animator is moving a rigged character from Maya to Unity. What is used most often?
cards.explain: FBX is the de facto standard for moving animated models between DCC tools and engines.

cards.task: A scene with a skeleton and a camera from an old program. Try at least three formats and see where the skeleton gets lost.

cards.q: Which Collada line sets the units?
cards.explain: unit meter="1" means one file unit equals one meter.

cards.q: A Collada file says <up_axis>Z_UP</up_axis>. What will a Y-up viewer do?
options: Rotate the model on import, if it reads the header correctly
cards.explain: The up axis is written in the file, so a good importer will rotate the model itself.

cards.q: What can FBX do? Select all.
cards.explain: It can do everything except be open.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: USD and USDZ
lessons.sub: Scenes built from layers and variants

cards.title: USD: Pixar’s scene language
cards.body:
Pixar open-sourced Universal Scene Description in 2016. It is not just “a file with a model” but a way to assemble huge scenes from hundreds of files.

Each department works in its own layer, and the final scene composes itself.

cards.title: Layers: who wins
cards.body:
Layers form a stack. If two layers set the same attribute, the stronger one wins: the one higher up.

The chair asset lives in one file, its placement in the scene in another, per-shot tweaks in a third. Nobody touches anyone else’s file.
cards.deep: USD strength order is remembered as LIVRPS: Local (opinions in layers), Inherits, VariantSets, References, Payloads, Specializes. A payload is deferred loading of heavy parts of a scene: you open a city and load only the block you need.

cards.task: Make the chair red without touching the asset file chair.usda.

cards.q: shot.usda says “red”, set.usda says “walnut”. The shot layer is higher. What will the chair be?
cards.explain: A stronger layer overrides the opinions of weaker ones.

cards.title: Variants
cards.body: A VariantSet is a set of mutually exclusive versions inside one asset: color, level of detail, “regular or bar stool”. Switch it and the scene changes, while the files stay the same.

cards.task: You need the walnut chair from set.usda in its bar variant.

cards.title: USDZ: USD for AR
cards.body:
USDZ is an uncompressed zip archive with USD files and textures inside. Apple uses it for AR Quick Look: open a link on an iPhone and the model appears on your table.

NVIDIA Omniverse is built entirely on USD. Since 2023 USD has been developed by the AOUSD alliance: Pixar, Apple, Adobe, Autodesk, NVIDIA.

cards.q: Why is USDZ an uncompressed zip?
options: The files inside can be read straight from the archive without unpacking
cards.explain: The files are also aligned to 64 bytes, so they can be memory-mapped and read right away.

cards.q: Where will you run into USD? Select all.
cards.explain: USD grew out of film and spread to AR and industrial “digital twins”.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A file with opinions about attributes
Bring in another file as part of the scene

lessons.title: Which format to choose
lessons.sub: The task decides, not fashion

cards.title: No best format, only the right one
cards.body:
3D printing needs only the shape: STL or 3MF.
Web and AR on Android: glTF/GLB. AR on iPhone: USDZ.
Animation between programs: FBX.
Scans: PLY.
Large studio scenes: USD.

cards.task: A part for 3D printing: only the shape matters. Pick the simplest format for printing.
A scan with a color at every point. Find a simple format, with no scenes or animation, that keeps vertex colors.
A character with PBR, animation and a camera for AR on iPhone. Everything has to survive.

cards.q: A model from Blender has to go on a website. Put the steps in order
items: Check the scale and up axis
cards.explain: Correct units first, then the delivery format, then compression and display.

cards.q: Match each task to a format
Why does an FBX → OBJ → FBX round trip damage a model?
options: OBJ stores no hierarchy or animation, so they are lost for good in the middle step
cards.explain: Conversion can only lose data. You cannot get it back.

cards.q: A client sent an STL and asks you to “color and animate it”. What do you say?
options: STL has no colors, UVs or skeleton: we need the source in a format with materials and animation
I will convert it to FBX and everything will appear
cards.explain: You can turn an STL into an FBX, but it will contain the same bare shape.

lessons.title: Final: mesh formats
lessons.sub: OBJ, STL, PLY, glTF, FBX, USD: test yourself

cards.task: A character has to move between programs without losses, but the format must be an open standard. Find it.

cards.q: Which format stores only triangles, with no color or units?
cards.explain: STL’s minimalism is both its strength and its weakness.

cards.q: Which PLY header line declares a color?
cards.code:
ply
format ascii 1.0
element vertex 8
property float x
property float y
property float z
property uchar red
end_header
cards.explain: property uchar red is the red component of the vertex color.

cards.q: How is GLB different from .gltf?
options: Everything is packed into one binary file
cards.explain: Same contents, different packaging.

cards.q: In USD, layer A is above layer B. Both set a color. Whose color wins?
cards.explain: Higher means stronger.

cards.q: What can OBJ not do? Select all.
cards.explain: OBJ does have UVs: the vt lines.

cards.task: A red bar stool, without editing chair.usda.

cards.q: Why is FBX a standard for animation but not for the web?
options: It is closed and built for exchange between programs, not for fast delivery to the screen
cards.explain: For the web there is glTF: open and ready to render.

cards.q: Which format has glTF almost replaced?
cards.explain: Both come from Khronos; glTF does the same job more simply and faster.

cards.q: Match them up

units.title: CAD: exact geometry
units.blurb: B-rep and NURBS instead of triangles, tessellation with tolerances, STEP and IGES, DWG, DXF, DWF and 3DM.

lessons.title: Mesh versus math
lessons.sub: B-rep, NURBS and a true circle

cards.title: A cylinder is a formula
cards.body:
In a mesh, a cylinder might be 64 triangles: it looks right, but it is an approximation.

In CAD, a cylinder is “a cylindrical surface with a 50 mm radius”: exact math. You can approximate it down to a micron, compute its volume exactly, or drill a hole dead center.

cards.title: B-rep: a boundary made of exact pieces
cards.body:
CAD describes a solid by its boundary: B-rep (boundary representation). Faces are pieces of exact surfaces: plane, cylinder, torus, NURBS. Edges are exact curves. Vertices are points.

On top of that there is topology: which face borders which, and along which edge.

cards.q: How many faces does a cylinder have in B-rep?
options: 3: two flat caps and one cylindrical face
cards.explain: The side is one face lying on an exact cylindrical surface, plus two flat ones.
cards.deep: Many geometry kernels (Parasolid, ACIS, Open CASCADE) cut the side face with a “seam”: a helper edge where the surface closes on itself. There are still three faces.

cards.title: NURBS: how to write any curve
cards.body:
NURBS (non-uniform rational B-splines) are curves and surfaces defined by control points with weights.

A plain Bézier curve cannot draw an exact circle, only something close. Give a control point a weight, and it can.

cards.task: An arc from three control points. Tune the middle point’s weight so the curve lies on the circle: error under 0.05 mm at a 50 mm radius.

cards.q: Which weight gave an exact quarter circle?
cards.explain: For an arc spanning angle θ, the middle weight is cos(θ/2). For 90° that is cos 45° ≈ 0.7071.

cards.q: With w = 1 the curve is…
options: A parabola: a plain Bézier curve that only approximates the circle
cards.explain: Without weights a quadratic Bézier curve is a piece of a parabola. The demo shows the error: about 3 mm at a 50 mm radius.

cards.q: What can you do exactly with CAD geometry but not with a mesh? Select all.
options: Get the exact radius of a hole
Build an exact fillet along an edge
Show it in a browser right away with no preparation
cards.explain: For display, though, CAD actually has to be turned into triangles. That is the next lesson.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A solid as a set of exact faces
Curves with control points and weights

lessons.title: Tessellation
lessons.sub: How finely to slice exact geometry

cards.title: To show CAD, you cut it into triangles
cards.body:
A GPU cannot draw “cylinder R50”. So before display, exact geometry is tessellated: turned into triangles.

The main question is how finely.

cards.task: Get the deviation from the true cylinder down to 0.1 mm or less, using no more than 260 triangles. Spin the cylinder with your finger.

cards.title: Chord and sagitta
cards.body:
A straight segment in place of an arc is a chord. The largest distance between the arc and the chord is the sagitta (chord height): r · (1 − cos(π / n)).

Double the segments and the error drops about fourfold, while the triangle count doubles.

cards.q: There were 32 segments, now there are 64. How did the error change?
cards.explain: For large n the sagitta ≈ r·π²/(2n²): the error falls with the square of the segment count.

cards.q: How does the size of a STEP file with this cylinder change between coarse and fine tessellation?
options: Not at all: STEP holds the formula, and tessellation happens later, at display or export
It grows with the triangle count
cards.explain: A STEP file’s size depends on the part’s complexity, not on display quality.

cards.title: Export settings
cards.body:
When CAD exports to STL or glTF, you set tolerances. Chordal deviation is how far triangles may stray from the surface, in millimeters. Angular deviation is how much neighboring triangles may differ in slope.

Tight tolerances give smooth and heavy; loose ones give light and angular.
cards.deep: The angular tolerance saves small features: for a Ø2 mm hole, a 0.1 mm chordal deviation gives only 7 segments, and the angle forces more. For the web, 0.1–0.5 mm is often enough. Huge assemblies get LODs (several levels of detail) or streaming formats like 3D Tiles.

cards.q: What grows when you tighten the tessellation tolerance? Select all.
options: Accuracy of the source CAD model
cards.explain: The source CAD model is exact already. Only its approximation changes.

cards.q: A CAD part’s path to a website
cards.explain: Formula → triangles → delivery format → screen.

cards.q: A Ø2 mm hole looks like a heptagon at a 0.1 mm chordal tolerance. What helps?
options: Add an angular tolerance: it forces small circles to be split finer
Save as OBJ instead of STL
cards.explain: The chordal tolerance suits large arcs; the angular one suits small ones.

lessons.title: STEP and IGES
lessons.sub: Neutral formats of mechanical engineering

cards.title: STEP: the common language of engineering
cards.body:
STEP is the international standard ISO 10303. Every serious CAD system understands it: SolidWorks, CATIA, NX, Creo, Inventor, Fusion, FreeCAD.

It holds exact surfaces (B-rep, NURBS) and assemblies, and the AP242 protocol adds dimensions and tolerances right on the model (PMI).
cards.deep: Application protocols (APs) are different “dialects” of STEP. AP203 is the design 3D model, AP214 is automotive (added colors and layers), and AP242 merged them and added PMI and data for drawing-free manufacturing (MBD).

cards.title: What STEP looks like
cards.body: It is text. Each line is an entity with its own number, and it refers to other numbers.

cards.q: Which line sets the 50 mm radius?
cards.explain: CYLINDRICAL_SURFACE(name, placement, radius) is our “cylinder with a 50 radius”.

cards.q: What does #13 refer to?
options: #12, the cylinder’s coordinate system: a point and an axis direction
cards.explain: #12 in turn refers to point #10 and direction #11. That is how STEP builds a model from small linked pieces.

cards.title: IGES: the ancestor
cards.body:
IGES appeared in the US in 1980 and was the main exchange format for a long time. The last version is 5.3 (1996).

It carries surfaces, but often handles solids and assemblies badly: after import you get “surfaces without a solid” that have to be stitched together. Today people use STEP instead.

cards.q: You imported an IGES and got a pile of separate surfaces with no volume. Why?
options: IGES often carries only surfaces without solid topology; you have to stitch them or use STEP
cards.explain: Without topology the program does not know the surfaces form a closed solid.

cards.q: What can STEP AP242 carry? Select all.
options: Dimensions and tolerances on the model (PMI)
cards.explain: STEP is about engineering, not games.

cards.q: A contractor asks for a part model “in a neutral format”. What do you send?
cards.explain: STEP keeps the exact geometry, and it can be edited further in any CAD system. STL is just triangles.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Dimensions and tolerances on the model

lessons.title: DWG, DXF, DWF and 3DM
lessons.sub: The AutoCAD and Rhino formats

cards.title: DWG: AutoCAD’s native format
cards.body:
DWG arrived with AutoCAD in 1982. The format is closed: Autodesk does not publish the spec. It has versions (for example AC1032 is the AutoCAD 2018 format), and an old AutoCAD will not open a newer file.

Other programs read DWG through the Open Design Alliance libraries, built by reverse engineering.

cards.title: DXF: the open text version
cards.body: Autodesk documents DXF publicly. It is text made of “group code, value” pairs: 0 is the object type, 8 is the layer, 10/20/30 are X, Y, Z of the first point, 11/21/31 of the second.

cards.q: Tap the X value of the line’s second end
cards.explain: Code 11 is the X of the second point, and the value comes on the next line: 5000.0.

cards.q: The drawing units are millimeters. How long is the line?
cards.explain: From (0, 0, 0) to (5000, 0, 0) is 5,000 mm, which is 5 meters.

cards.title: DWF and 3DM
cards.body:
DWF (Design Web Format) is a lightweight Autodesk format “for viewing and printing”, like PDF for drawings: you can look and mark up, but not edit.

3DM is Rhino’s native format. The openNURBS library for reading and writing it is open, so many programs understand 3DM.

cards.q: The client only needs to view the drawing and leave markups, with no editing rights. What do you send?
cards.explain: DWG and DXF are source files and can be edited. DWF is for viewing.

cards.q: Which are true about DWG? Select all.
options: A newer DWG may not open in an older AutoCAD
cards.explain: DXF is the text one. DWG is binary and is nobody’s standard but Autodesk’s.

cards.q: Fill in the group code for the layer
cards.explain: Code 8 is the layer name. 62 is the color number, 10 is the X coordinate.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: Final: exact geometry
lessons.sub: B-rep, tessellation, STEP and DWG: test yourself

cards.task: Prepare the cylinder for the web: deviation of 0.1 mm or less and no more than 260 triangles.

cards.q: How is a cylinder in STEP different from a cylinder in GLB?
options: STEP has the formula “radius 50 mm”; GLB has a set of triangles
cards.explain: STEP stores the exact surface; GLB stores an approximation of it.

cards.task: Turn the Bézier curve into an exact quarter circle.

cards.q: The segment count went up 3 times. The tessellation error dropped by about…
cards.explain: The error falls with the square of the segment count.

cards.q: Where is the exact surface here?
cards.explain: SPHERICAL_SURFACE with radius 25 is an exact sphere. The rest is its coordinate system.

cards.q: Which of these are exact CAD geometry? Select all.
cards.explain: STL and GLB are triangles.

cards.q: A drawing from a new AutoCAD will not open for a colleague with an old one. What do you do?
options: Save to an older DWG version or send a DXF
cards.explain: AutoCAD can “Save As” older DWG versions.

cards.q: What does the angular tolerance give you in tessellation?
options: Small circles get split finely enough even when the chordal deviation is already met
cards.explain: The angle limits how much neighboring triangles can differ in slope.

cards.q: Match them up

units.title: BIM: buildings made of smart objects
units.blurb: Objects with properties instead of meshes, IFC from the inside, RVT, PLN and Navisworks, clash detection and BCF issues.

lessons.title: What BIM is
lessons.sub: A building as a database with a 3D view

cards.title: Not just shape, but meaning
cards.body:
In BIM (Building Information Modeling) a building is assembled not from triangles but from objects: wall, door, window, slab. Each one has a type, a storey, materials, a fire rating, a manufacturer, a cost.

It is a database that happens to have a 3D view.

cards.title: Put simply
cards.body:
A mesh is a photo of a finished LEGO model: you see what it looks like.

BIM is the LEGO set itself, with instructions: every brick knows what it is, what it clips onto and how much it costs.

cards.task: Find the doors on the second floor, then tap “Save as GLB” and see what is left.

cards.q: What was left after saving as GLB?
options: Only geometry: the properties and relationships are gone
cards.explain: GLB is a display format. It has no idea what a “door” or a “storey” is.

cards.q: What does a BIM door object know that a mesh does not? Select all.
cards.explain: A mesh knows the look too. But meaning, place in the building and properties belong to BIM alone.

cards.q: Why do builders need “smart” objects?
options: To compute quantities and cost, check codes, find clashes and hand data over to facility management
cards.explain: Schedules, cost estimates and timelines all come out of a BIM model. Geometry is only part of the data.

cards.title: Who works with BIM
cards.body:
The architect, the structural engineer, the HVAC, plumbing and electrical engineers: each in their own program.

To bring it all together you need a common language, IFC, and a federated model for coordination.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: IFC from the inside
lessons.sub: The building tree, properties and GlobalId

cards.title: IFC: an open buildingSMART standard
cards.body:
IFC (Industry Foundation Classes) is maintained by buildingSMART and is the ISO 16739 standard.

The most common versions are IFC2x3 and IFC4. IFC4.3 added infrastructure: roads, bridges, railways.

cards.title: The building tree
cards.body:
Everything sits in a spatial structure: IfcProject → IfcSite → IfcBuilding → IfcBuildingStorey (a floor) → elements: IfcWall, IfcDoor, IfcWindow, IfcSlab.

Properties are grouped into property sets. For example, Pset_WallCommon: FireRating, IsExternal, LoadBearing.

cards.task: Filter for the doors on the second floor.

cards.q: How many doors are on the second floor?
cards.explain: Two interior doors and one to the balcony.

cards.task: Find all walls that have a fire rating set, and open the properties of one of them.

cards.q: Arrange the IFC spatial structure from top to bottom
cards.explain: Project → site → building → storey → element.

cards.title: An .ifc file is STEP
cards.body: The most common IFC encoding is the same ISO 10303-21 text format used by STEP in mechanical engineering: numbered lines that refer to each other.
cards.deep: A GlobalId is a 128-bit GUID written as 22 characters in a special base64 alphabet. It is how an object is recognized across model updates and in BCF issues. There are also ifcXML and ifcZIP, and buildingSMART is developing IFC5 with a different, more web-friendly design.

cards.q: Which line sets the fire rating?
cards.explain: IFCPROPERTYSINGLEVALUE named FireRating with the value REI 90. Line 4 attaches the property set to wall #120.

cards.q: What does IFC contain? Select all.
cards.explain: IFC is a snapshot for exchange. History and program internals stay in the program’s native file.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: The “element is on this floor” link

lessons.title: Native formats and coordination
lessons.sub: RVT, PLN, Navisworks and clashes

cards.title: Every program keeps its own
cards.body:
RVT is Revit’s native format, and it is closed. A file from a newer Revit will not open in an older one. PLN is Archicad’s native format.

The native format has everything: history, families, views, drawing sheets. IFC has only what is needed for exchange.

cards.title: Navisworks: the federated model
cards.body:
Disciplines are modeled in different programs, and Navisworks brings them into one scene.

NWC is a cache generated from each source file. NWD is a published federated model with all geometry inside, easy to view and check.
cards.deep: There is also NWF, a “list of links” to the source files: on open, Navisworks pulls in fresh NWCs. Clash detection (Clash Detective) lives in Navisworks Manage; in the cloud, services like Autodesk Construction Cloud take its place.

cards.task: Run a hard clash check between disciplines.

cards.q: How many hard clashes were found?
cards.explain: Duct D-7 runs straight through both beams.

cards.task: Pipes need 50 mm of clearance for insulation. Check with a 50 mm tolerance.

cards.q: Why did one more clash show up with 50 mm clearance?
options: Pipe P-4 runs 10 mm below a beam: no intersection, but the insulation will not fit
cards.explain: This is a “soft” clash: the elements do not intersect, but the required clearance is violated.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all.
options: NWD is a federated model for viewing and checking
NWC is generated from source files
cards.explain: IFC carries only exchange data. PLN is Archicad’s format.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Navisworks cache of one source file

lessons.title: BCF: issues, not models
lessons.sub: How to say “the problem is right here”

cards.title: An issue instead of a model
cards.body:
Finding a clash is only half the job. You have to hand it to whoever will fix it.

BCF (BIM Collaboration Format, from buildingSMART) is not a model but an issue: a title, a status, an assignee, a camera viewpoint, a screenshot and the GlobalIds of the elements. The model itself is not inside.

cards.task: Find the clash between duct D-7 and beam B-12 and create a BCF issue for it.

cards.q: Which line points to a specific element in the model?
cards.code:
<Topic Guid="7c1e…" TopicStatus="Open">
  <Title>Duct D-7 × Beam B-12</Title>
</Topic>
<Component IfcGuid="0Np4AyS5p7Th2Wg9Va4Ij3"/>
<PerspectiveCamera>…</PerspectiveCamera>
cards.explain: IfcGuid is the same GlobalId from IFC. Any program can use it to find the duct in its own copy of the model.

cards.q: Why is BCF tiny even when the model weighs gigabytes?
options: It has no geometry: only GlobalId references, a camera and a screenshot
cards.explain: Every participant has their own copy of the model. BCF tells them where to look in it.

cards.title: Inside a .bcfzip
cards.body:
It is a zip archive. Each issue gets a folder with markup.bcf (XML: title, comments, status), viewpoint.bcfv (camera, visible and selected elements) and snapshot.png.

There is also the BCF API for exchanging issues through the cloud, with no files.

cards.q: The life of one issue
items: The coordinator created a BCF with a camera and GlobalIds
The engineer opened the BCF and saw the same spot
They fixed the model and closed the issue
cards.explain: BCF connects people and programs without sending the model itself.

cards.q: What is inside a BCF? Select all.
cards.explain: Everything except the model.

cards.q: Will a BCF open in a different program from the one that created it?
options: Yes, if it supports BCF: it is an open buildingSMART standard
No, only in the same one
cards.explain: BCF is supported by Revit, Archicad, Solibri, BIMcollab, Navisworks (via plugins) and many others.

lessons.title: Final: the smart building
lessons.sub: IFC, coordination and BCF: test yourself

cards.task: Filter for the windows on the second floor.

cards.q: How is IFC different from a GLB with the same geometry?
options: In IFC, objects have a type, a storey, properties and relationships
cards.explain: GLB knows what it looks like. IFC knows what it is.

cards.task: Find all clashes with a 150 mm clearance.

cards.q: Which line is the wall itself?
cards.explain: IFCWALL with a GlobalId. #130 is its geometry, #140 is a property.

cards.q: Why does IFC open in both Revit and Archicad?
options: It is the open standard ISO 16739
cards.explain: IFC was created precisely for exchange between different programs.

cards.q: Which of these are closed native formats? Select all.
cards.explain: IFC and BCF are open buildingSMART standards.

cards.q: A coordinator wants to tell an engineer “there is a pipe in this beam”. What do they send?
options: A BCF issue with a camera and GlobalIds
A screenshot in a chat app with no element references
cards.explain: BCF opens exactly that view for the engineer and highlights the right elements.

cards.q: The IFC spatial structure
cards.explain: From top to bottom.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: How to find an object in any program

units.title: Point clouds
units.blurb: Site scans: points, intensity and classes, LAS and LAZ, E57, PTS/XYZ, ReCap and the scan-to-BIM path.

lessons.title: What a point cloud is
lessons.sub: Millions of points instead of surfaces

cards.title: Millions of points instead of surfaces
cards.body:
A laser scanner stands on a construction site and “fires” a beam at everything around it. Each reflection is a point: x, y, z, sometimes a color and the strength of the return.

There are no surfaces, only points, and lots of them: millions or billions. Like a dot drawing made with a marker: from afar you see a house, up close only dots.

cards.task: Cycle through the color modes: what data does each point store? Look at at least three.

cards.q: What is a point’s intensity?
options: How strongly the beam reflected off the surface
cards.explain: Glass and wet asphalt reflect weakly, white plaster strongly. That is why the windows look dark in the demo.

cards.title: Point classes
cards.body:
In LAS clouds each point can have a class: 2 is ground, 5 is high vegetation, 6 is building, 9 is water.

Algorithms and people assign classes so that later you can, say, keep only the ground and build the terrain.

cards.q: You need to build the terrain of a site. Which points do you keep?
cards.explain: A digital terrain model (DTM) is built from ground points. Trees and houses get in the way.

cards.q: Where do point clouds come from? Select all.
options: Lidar on a drone or plane
The lidar in an iPhone Pro
cards.explain: STL is already triangles. You can sample a cloud from it, but that is not a scan.

cards.q: What makes a point cloud awkward to display compared with a mesh?
options: There are no surfaces: up close you see gaps, and there are billions of points
It is always black and white
cards.explain: That is why big clouds are shown in pieces: nearby areas in detail, distant ones thinned out.
cards.deep: For the web, clouds are cut into an octree of detail levels, for example the Potree format or 3D Tiles. The viewer loads only visible and nearby nodes.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: LAS, LAZ and E57
lessons.sub: Laser scanning standards

cards.title: LAS: the laser scanning standard
cards.body:
LAS is specified by ASPRS, the American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing. It is a binary file: a header and point records of equal size.

There are several record formats. For example, format 7 in LAS 1.4: coordinates, intensity, return number, class, GPS time and color, 36 bytes per point.
cards.deep: Coordinates are stored as 32-bit integers with a scale and offset from the header: X = Xrecord × scale + offset. That way millimeter precision fits in 4 bytes even for coordinates hundreds of kilometers out.

cards.title: LAZ: the same LAS, compressed
cards.body:
LAZ (LASzip) compresses LAS losslessly, usually down to 7–20% of the size. Decompress it and you get the original LAS, byte for byte.

That is why scan archives are almost always kept in LAZ.

cards.task: A 100-million-point scan has to fit into 1 GB. Pick a format in the calculator.

cards.q: Why did LAZ fit while LAS did not?
options: LAZ compresses the same data losslessly several times over
cards.explain: Nothing is lost: neighboring points are similar, and the algorithm encodes the difference between them.

cards.title: E57: the open scanner format
cards.body:
E57 is the ASTM E2807 standard. It stores not only points but the structure of the survey: where the scanner stood, each station’s point grid, and panoramic photos.

It is handy for exchange between software from different scanner makers.

cards.q: You need to hand over scans along with panoramic photos from each station. What do you pick?
cards.explain: LAS and XYZ store only points. E57 can hold images and station positions too.

cards.q: How much space do 10 million points at 36 bytes take?
Which are true? Select all.
options: A LAS point can have a class
cards.explain: LAS is binary, and LAZ gives the data back byte for byte.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Open ASTM format with scans and photos

lessons.title: PTS, XYZ and ReCap
lessons.sub: Plain text, Autodesk projects and scan-to-BIM

cards.title: As simple as it gets: XYZ and PTS
cards.body:
XYZ is text: each line holds x y z, sometimes r g b too.
PTS (a Leica format): the first line is the point count, then x y z, intensity and r g b.

Anything can open it, but it is huge and slow: every digit is a separate byte.

cards.q: Which PTS line is the point count?
cards.explain: The first line says how many points follow. The fourth number on each line is intensity, then the color.

cards.q: Why are PTS and XYZ so big?
options: Every digit is written as a text character: a point takes dozens of bytes instead of 20–36
cards.explain: “12.402” is 6 bytes as text, while in LAS the same coordinate is a 4-byte integer.

cards.title: RCP and RCS: point clouds in Autodesk
cards.body:
ReCap is Autodesk’s point cloud software. RCS is a single scan converted into a fast indexed format. RCP is a project that references a set of RCS files.

RCP is what you load into Revit, Navisworks and AutoCAD.

cards.q: A colleague sent only an .rcp, and the cloud will not open. Why?
options: RCP is a project of references; the points themselves live in .rcs files that were not included
cards.explain: Same story as an OBJ without textures: a file of references without the things it references.

cards.title: From scan to BIM model
cards.body:
Scans from different stations are stitched into one cloud: that is registration. Then the cloud is cleaned and classified, and walls and pipes are modeled from it: that is scan-to-BIM.

This is how teams check whether everything was built as designed, or model an old building before renovation.

cards.q: Put the scan-to-BIM steps in order
items: Registration: stitch scans into one cloud
Modeling BIM objects from the cloud
cards.explain: From points to smart objects, and back to checking.

cards.task: A billion points: fit into 10 GB.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: Final: which format do you need
lessons.sub: The whole course mixed together, from STL to LAZ

cards.task: Fit 100 million points into 1 GB.

cards.q: Match each task to a format
pairs: Show a model on a website
Send a part to another CAD system
Move a BIM model between programs

cards.q: More tasks

cards.task: A scan with vertex colors: find a simple format, with no scenes or animation, that keeps the color.

cards.q: Which format stores exact geometry rather than triangles?
cards.explain: STEP holds B-rep and NURBS. The others are triangles or points.

cards.q: A LAS point has class 6. What is it?
cards.explain: 2 is ground, 5 is high vegetation, 6 is building, 9 is water.

cards.q: Which formats are open standards? Select all.
cards.explain: RVT and DWG are closed Autodesk formats.

cards.q: To show a STEP file in a browser, you need to…
options: Tessellate it into triangles and save it as, say, GLB
cards.explain: Browsers draw triangles, not formulas.

cards.q: You got an .rcp without .rcs files and an .obj without an .mtl. What do they have in common?
options: They are files of references: without the files they point to, the data is incomplete
cards.explain: External references are the top cause of “broken” transfers in 3D. The fix is single-file packages: GLB, USDZ, NWD, E57.

cards.q: From construction site to issue
cards.explain: The course’s four worlds in one chain.
